sentences.text: The genus Eremopezus contains only one known species, Eremopezus eocaenus, an enormous bird that was likely flightless.
Its name translates to 'walking hermit,' combining Greek words for a solitary place and the act of walking.
This gigantic bird possessed well-developed legs extending from the lower leg to the midfoot, along with widely divergent toes capable of flexing through a wide range of positions.
C. W. Andrews described the genus in 1904 based on a distal left tibiotarsus specimen.
Fossils were discovered in the Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation near Faiyum, Egypt, specifically at the Qasr el Sagha escarpment north of Lake Birket Qarun.
Initially, scientists believed Eremopezus was a ratite closely related to the elephant birds of Madagascar, but deep ligamental pits on its distal condyles distinguish it from those birds.
Furthermore, the tarsometatarsus of Eremopezus resembles that of general ratites like emus or ostriches rather than elephant birds.
Because its closest relatives are unknown, the genus may belong to a distinct family called Eremopezidae.
The animal lived during the Late Eocene epoch, in rocks deposited between approximately 36 and 33 million years ago during the Priabonian stage.
Researchers suggest it behaved similarly to secretarybirds and shoebills within the swamps of the Jebel Qatrani Formation.

It is debated whether Eremopezus represents a separate example of ratite bodyplan origins or is a flightless neognath, and if it was a palaeognath, it is considered the most unusual one known to date.

Additionally, there is a debate regarding whether Eremopezus possessed a hook or 'nail' on its bill tip if it was a pelecaniform, and robust conclusions about its habits remain impossible without further fossil data.
There is also a debate regarding whether certain fossil eggshells from the Maghreb belong to Eremopezus or to ostriches.
